profile.research_note: [batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This CyrusOne campus sits in Chandler, Arizona. Wikipedia coverage of CyrusOne states the company acquired 55.9 acres in Chandler in September 2011 for data center construction, part of its early 2010s national expansion under Cincinnati Bell ownership. CyrusOne was founded in July 2000 by David Ferdman and Larry Bursten and was taken private in 2022 when Kohlberg Kravis Roberts and Global Infrastructure Partners acquired it for 15 billion dollars. No building specific address or individual MW figures were located in available sourcing this session.

reading.body:
The CyrusOne Chandler campus publishes 169 MW of IT capacity across eight co-located buildings, making it the largest published data center facility in Arizona and representing 33 percent of the state's 512 MW of published capacity. The campus holds certifications for financial services compliance, healthcare data handling, federal systems hosting, and physical security standards. Technical space totals 2 million square feet.

At 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, 169 MW of IT load translates to approximately 4,200 racks. At 8 accelerators per rack, a common configuration for GPU-based training clusters, this implies potential headroom for roughly 33,600 accelerators, though the operator publishes neither the rack count nor the customer mix, and actual AI utilization depends on tenant configuration. The campus certifications qualify it for regulated finance and healthcare workloads but do not indicate whether current tenants are AI operators.

Arizona ranks fifth nationally in published data center capacity, with 56 mapped facilities statewide but only four with published power figures. Chandler sits in the Phoenix metropolitan area, which has become a secondary hub for U.S. data center investment after the Bay Area and Northern Virginia. Whether this campus will matter to AI scaling depends on whether its tenant roster shifts toward training operations and whether grid and cooling constraints in Arizona's high-heat climate permit sustained utilization at full capacity, neither of which is published.
